title: No action cards: an offer is a tool call that the user approves
Personalized pages are not built
Feature suggestions come from a skill over the local catalogue
A translation is read from the log by the host, logged before it is sent, and settled once
The web translation endpoints are a registered sender, and no provider is preselected
All-prompts titles are a provider in the title seam, selected by one config field
The badge skill is not shipped
Config ids and persisted names carry no maturity marker
Text is translated through a seam, and every request and result is in the session
Web translation sends one paragraph to one chosen endpoint, and only with a permit
A reader switches an expanded reasoning block between original and translation
A session's title can follow the whole conversation
The model can name the optional feature that answers a wish, and an owner switches it on
Two optional bundles switch the features on, and a stock installation has none of it
The translations fold maps an identity to its successful outcome and skips invalid records
A translation request is flushed before dispatch and settled by exactly one outcome, with no fallback and no session activation
The text to translate comes from the committed event, excludes code, and is split safely
Web translation makes no request without a permit and a chosen provider, and stops at the off-switch
The two web wire shapes encode and decode as golden files, and a bad body is one classified error
The reasoning translation fragments show every toolbar state and always keep the original reachable
The all-prompts provider schedules one generation per own prompt and leaves an unchanged title alone
The optional-features skill lists only optional bundles, names where an owner switches one on, and no tool in scope can enable one
The optional bundles compose as disabled groups, a stock profile sends nothing, and no dropped component exists
A real model translates reasoning, and the log shows the request before the outcome
Web translation sends nothing until chosen, sends one paragraph when chosen, and stops at the off-switch
A real model keeps a fitting title and replaces one the conversation has outgrown
The model points to an optional feature, and only the owner can switch it on

reason: The package turns a fenced action-card block in an answer into a card with state, user actions and a status notice. The Go design does not build this mechanism: the one surviving offer (turning on an optional feature) is a tool call that the guarded pipeline sends to approval, which already guarantees that nothing runs before the user's yes and that the model learns the answer. The cost of dropping is that an offer is no longer deferred below the answer.

The browser half draws the card frame and hides every action-card block. With no cards there is no frame to draw and no block to hide; an approval is rendered by the interaction region that areas A17 and C4 own.

On a click the package has a Creator subagent write a JavaScript plugin with a host half and a browser half, validates it and installs it into the profile for every session. The Go host loads no code into its process (DH-ADR-4), has no client plugin runtime (DH-ADR-3) and a plugin process cannot add UI, so there is no artifact the feature could produce.
This is the card body of the personalized-page feature: location picker, cost notice, progress, Undo and Restore. It has no subject once the feature itself is not built.

Upstream gives the model a local catalogue of shipped optional bundles through a skill and enables one from a card click. The source shows no remote service and no dependency on a plugin market (src/skill.ts:11-22). Go keeps the skill and the local catalogue as the feature-guide component and replaces the card click by the approval of a plugin_manager set_enabled call.

The card body shows a bundle's title and description with Enable and Not now. In Go the same choice is the approval prompt for one set_enabled call, rendered by the host; the catalogue text reaches the user through the model's answer and the settings page.

The package is a bundle patch that inserts six rows: the card service, the card frame and two features with their card bodies. Nothing in it personalises anything. Go ships the optional bundle feature-guide with one entry, the successor of the plugin-recommendation rows; the other four rows are dropped with cards and personalized pages.

The translation service is kept as a seam with a provider registry: a model provider (an auxiliary logged call on a configured route) and the two web endpoints. Requests and results stay in the session, now as declared event types with exactly one outcome per request, a fold as the lookup index, and text read by the host from the committed event.

The React wrapper around the reasoning body and its remote controller become server-rendered fragments: a toolbar and translated paragraphs contributed to the reasoning body, two host routes and a view preference. The host, not the browser, splits the text and names what is translated.
The bundle becomes the embedded optional bundle reasoning-translation: one disabled group that inserts four entries. Unlike upstream it preselects no provider, so turning it on sends nothing.

The package is one fixed skill that tells the model to add a powered-by-dsh badge, with upstream's project address, logo and a remote image address, to documents and to every pull request. A reimplementation does not ship another project's attribution as its own, and a SKILL.md in a user or project skill directory gives the same ability.
The bundle only switches the badge skill on. It follows its feature: with no badge skill there is nothing to switch.

The package is a second title provider with a different cadence. It is folded into the title seam of area A06 as the provider all-prompts: two prompt texts and an unchanged-title rule, with A06's generator making, logging and settling the call.

The bundle swaps title providers by disabling another bundle's row, which a Go optional bundle may not do because it may only insert. Its job is folded into one config field, title.Config.Provider, with the provider mounted as an ordinary entry.

The bundle switches on the plugin-index reader and its Discover tab. DH-ADR-13 decides that plugins come from local directories with no discovery or download, and area A21 builds no index reader, so there is nothing for the bundle to mount.

The model is not told when its block creates no card. In Go there is no block: an offer is a tool call, and every tool call returns a result to the model (allowed, denied or an error), so a failed offer is always visible to it.

The host scans blocks line by line while the browser's Markdown parser hides them, and the two disagree in block quotes, nested lists, HTML and math. Go reads no action-card block and hides none, so there are not two readers to disagree; such a block is shown as an ordinary code block.
The limit is about sessions recorded with a removed upstream tool. The Go store reads no upstream session (DH-ADR-2), and Go has no card records at all, so no old record can be skipped.

An invalid card still replaces an earlier unstarted card. Go has no replacement rule: a call with unknown or invalid arguments is refused by the pipeline's schema check and leaves every other pending approval untouched.

Cards exist only in the main conversation because only a live root can act on one. A tool call needs no live-root rule of its own: whether a subagent may propose set_enabled follows from its preset's tools, and who may answer the approval is area A17's rule.
Only one card per turn is offered and a later card replaces an earlier one. Each proposed tool call is its own approval, so a second offer does not replace the first.

Refusal reasons are free strings that each browser body must know. The outcome of an offered action in Go is the pipeline's closed decision set plus errors from the one domain/reason table of design.md section 4.8.

Each kind validates the same details with a host schema and a separate browser schema that must change together. Go has no browser schema: the arguments of the tool call are one Go struct validated once by the pipeline.
A card whose experiment ships no browser body offers only Not now. There are no card bodies in Go; an approval prompt is rendered by the host for every tool the same way.
The turn tail shows one card per turn. No card is drawn in Go, and several approvals in one turn are listed together by the interaction region.
Only the first proposal of a turn appears as a card. In Go each proposal is a tool call with its own approval, so a second proposal in a turn is not lost.

The card reserves a placeholder line because the React client fetches the catalogue text after it has drawn the card. This is a client-side rendering artifact: a host-rendered fragment is written with the text it already has, and no card is drawn at all.

A card keeps showing a recorded decision that later changes on the Plugins page have made untrue. Go keeps no card status: the transcript shows a tool result as a past fact, and the current state is read from area A21's manager wherever it is displayed.

After a refused or lost browser lookup the Enable button returns only on Try again. There is no browser lookup in Go: the host validates the feature id when the call is proposed and renders the prompt itself.

A card whose plugin left the catalogue falls back to the title the model proposed. In Go a call that names an unknown feature id is an error result to the model, and nothing is shown to the user as an offer.

Eligibility excludes missing packages and third-party registries. In Go the catalogue lists embedded optional bundles, which are in the binary and cannot be missing, and no registry exists to exclude (DH-ADR-13). Plugins the operator added are visible through plugin_manager list.

Half of the limit is removed and half is kept: a suggestion no longer needs the exact live root agent, because it is a skill plus a tool call, but there is still no unsolicited discovery of opportunities.
justification: Kept on purpose: suggesting a feature the user did not ask about would need either a background model call over the conversation or a stored profile of the user's behaviour, and neither is wanted in a product whose rule is that nothing is collected or sent by default (DH-ADR-9). DH-D-XMISC-5 builds the on-request path. The stage is a placeholder because the implementation plan is not written.

reason: A recorded card decision does not follow later changes made on the Plugins page. Go records no card decision: the log holds the tool call and its result as history, and the skill catalogue is rebuilt from the live composition every time it is loaded.

The catalogue reports one enabled flag per bundle, so a bundle with one of its rows switched off still reads as enabled. The Go catalogue row has three states: on, off, and partly when the group is on and at least one of its entries is disabled.
The Creator's restrictions are found by walking live subagent agents and break when an intermediate agent has exited. No Creator job exists in Go, so there is no restriction to look up.
Only new plugins can be created and Restore has no version history. Nothing is created or restored in Go because the feature is not built.

Generated code runs with the Creator's permissions and package validation is not a sandbox. Go installs no generated code into the host; a model-written plugin is area A22's separate, confined process that is approved per session.
Source directories and profile copies are left behind after success, failure, cancellation and Undo. With no creation there is no directory to leave behind.
A creation run has no timeout. No creation run exists in Go.
The brief shown on the creation card is written by the model and existing data travels in a separate field. There is no creation card and no brief in Go.
Creation receipts on old cards do not follow later manual changes on the Plugins page. Go stores no creation receipt.
The bundle page lists four supporting card rows that it cannot mark or hide. The Go bundle feature-guide has exactly one entry, so there is no supporting row.

This README bullet is only a pointer to the limitations of two other upstream packages, which exists because upstream documents each npm package on its own page. It states no limit of its own; the units it points at (creation-recommendations 1 to 5 and plugin-recommendations 1 to 4) each have their own row.
There is no official plugin index, so Discover lists only sources the user adds. Go has no index reader and no Discover page at all: plugins are local directories the operator places.

The badge is usable only by presets that load skills. No badge skill is shipped; a user's own skill file follows the ordinary rule that a preset must mount the skill tool, which area A14 states for every skill.

The limit is about a preview image in the documentation folder of an upstream npm bundle package, shown by upstream's plugin page, that has no dark variant. The Go design ships neither that package nor a per-bundle preview image.

The provider offers one fixed skill that cannot be customised. Go ships no fixed badge skill; a badge of any wording is a SKILL.md in the user's or project's skill directory, read by area A14's filesystem provider.
The shipped badge text depends on a remote image service. Nothing the Go binary ships names that service, so the dependency is gone.

The Google and Bing anonymous endpoints may reject requests or disappear. The Go design keeps both as optional web providers, so the limit stays for a user who chooses one; no fallback to another provider is kept as a rule, not as a defect.
justification: The endpoints belong to other vendors and no design choice here can make them reliable. The harm is bounded: they are off until the user turns the sender on and chooses one (DH-ADR-XMISC-5), the model provider needs no third endpoint, and a failure is one logged outcome with Retry. The owner is asked in section 10 whether to ship them at all. The stage is a placeholder because the implementation plan is not written.

reason: Half of the limit is removed and half is kept: code blocks, math and tables are never sent to a translator, so code examples cannot be changed, but the inline formatting of translated prose may still change.
justification: Machine translation of prose can move or drop inline markup whatever the provider, and checking it would need a second parser pass that guesses intent. The original is one click away in every state, which DH-T-XMISC-6 asserts. DH-D-XMISC-1 builds the exclusion of code. The stage is a placeholder because the implementation plan is not written.

reason: The limit changes form and stays: a session that no live agent holds for writing in this host, such as a finished subagent session, shows saved translations but cannot get a new one. Go reports it as a plain reason instead of a translation failure.
justification: A new translation appends two events and so needs the session's lease. Upstream's remedy, activating the session to write the record, ran preset start-up hooks and could append model-visible context only so that a reader could see a translation; that is removed on purpose (DH-ADR-XMISC-4). Whether a host component may append log-only events to a session nobody holds is asked of areas A01 and A05 in section 10; a yes removes the limit. The stage is a placeholder because the implementation plan is not written.

reason: Saved translations are experimental plugin records kept on a best-effort basis across format changes. In Go they are declared event types with a payload version and converters like any other persisted type (DH-ADR-PERSISTENCE-6). The collapsed preview staying original is kept on purpose: translating it would send text before the reader asked.
Whether the two web endpoints can be reached from mainland China depends on the user's network. The Go web providers use the same endpoints, so the same uncertainty holds for them.
justification: Reachability of a third party's endpoint from a given network is outside the design. What the design gives: the one egress proxy policy applies to these requests, an unreachable endpoint is one classified failure, and the model provider translates through a route the user already reaches. DH-E-XMISC-2 records an unreachable endpoint as open, never as passed. The stage is a placeholder because the implementation plan is not written.

reason: The same limit as client-ui-cot-translation.2, stated on the bundle page: collapsed summaries stay original and translation may change formatting. Code blocks, math and tables are no longer sent; inline formatting of prose may still change; the original stays reachable.
justification: Kept for the reasons given for client-ui-cot-translation.2: a formatting change is inherent to machine translation of prose. Leaving the collapsed summary untranslated is deliberate, because expanding the block is the reader's request to translate and nothing is sent before it. The stage is a placeholder because the implementation plan is not written.

reason: Half of the limit is removed and half is kept: saved translations are no longer best-effort records, because they are declared event types, but the anonymous endpoints may still fail, limit requests or change their response format.
justification: The endpoints are another vendor's and stay outside the project's control. A changed response format is caught by the strict decoder as one classified error, and the golden wire tests of DH-T-XMISC-5 show which shape the build expects. DH-ADR-XMISC-5 keeps them off until chosen. The stage is a placeholder because the implementation plan is not written.

reason: The two browser endpoints are unofficial, with no guarantee of availability, quota, format or regional reachability. The Go web providers call the same endpoints, so the limit stays for whoever chooses them.
justification: No design can give a guarantee the endpoint's owner does not give. The Go design makes them the second choice, not the default: no provider is preselected, the sender is off until turned on, and the model provider is the path with a supported API. The owner is asked in section 10 whether to ship the web providers at all; dropping them would resolve this unit. The stage is a placeholder because the implementation plan is not written.

reason: Paid translation charges on every miss with best-effort record retention. In Go each model translation leaves a request event and one outcome event with usage, so every charge is in the log, and the records are declared types with versions. That no route falls back to another is kept as a rule (DH-O-8), not a defect.

Consumers own session activation, paragraph scheduling, input splitting and display fallback, and bad language tags fail only at the provider. In Go the service owns reading, splitting and scheduling because the host renders the transcript, nothing activates a session, and a tag that does not parse is refused before any request. One request per miss with no automatic retry is kept as a rule.

Every fragment lookup scans the whole session log and rebuilds an index. In Go the index is the registered fold translations, kept current as events commit and checkpointed by area A06's registry, so a lookup reads one event.

A failed or interrupted attempt is left as a request record with nothing that closes it. In Go every request gets exactly one outcome event (ok, failed, cancelled or interrupted, the last appended by the next lease holder), so an unfinished attempt cannot be mistaken for a pending one. A retry is still a new request, which is what an append-only log requires.

One malformed translation record, or a result without its request, makes every lookup in that session fail. In Go a payload is validated when it is appended, and the fold skips an event it cannot use and reports it in the fold status while other lookups keep working.

Input over the byte limit fails and keeps the old title, with no policy for very long sessions. Area A06's generator, which this provider uses, reduces over-limit input by keeping the first prompt and the newest prompts that fit, so a long session still gets a title from a stated subset.

Every eligible human message is included with equal weight and there is no configurable weighting or filtering. Go keeps this under the byte limit; over it, the generator's reduction favours the first and the newest prompts.
justification: A weighting or filter setting would be a knob without evidence of which weighting gives better titles, and the reduction rule already decides what matters when space runs out. DH-D-XMISC-4 builds the provider on that rule. The stage is a placeholder because the implementation plan is not written.

reason: Keeping an adequate title is an instruction to the model, not a deterministic check, so the model may still reword it. Go keeps the instruction and adds the one deterministic part available: a returned title equal to the current one after normalisation appends no new title event.
justification: Whether two different titles mean the same is a judgement only a model can make, so no deterministic semantic check exists to build. A user who wants a fixed title pins it, which stops automatic titles. DH-E-XMISC-3 observes the behaviour with a real model and reports repeated runs. The stage is a placeholder because the implementation plan is not written.

reason: The title input budget rejects oversized input instead of shortening it, and a failure silently keeps the old title. Area A06's generator shortens over-limit input and writes one attempt event for every failure, so the kept title has a logged reason.

view.Config replaces it with the same two fields, Provider and TargetLanguage (default auto). Provider has no default: upstream's preselected bing is not kept, so that turning the feature on chooses no receiver.

Three structs replace the one schema, one per component: translate.Config (MaxTextRunes 4000, Timeout 10 s), model.Config (Route, Model, MaxOutputTokens 8192, Timeout 60 s) and web.Config (the two endpoints, MaxResponseBytes 1048576, and a new Enabled field that is the sender's own setting, default false). The provider field moves to the view's config.

The provider has no config struct of its own. Its fields (target lengths, input bytes, output tokens, timeout, route) are the fields of area A06's title.GeneratorConfig, which serves every title provider, and title.Config.Provider set to all-prompts selects it.

ctx.actionCards registers card kinds, records decisions and takes user actions on cards. The card mechanism is not built, so no service key replaces it; approvals go through area A17's interaction registry.

ctx.cotTranslation is a remote controller with two methods for the browser. There is no service in Go: limits becomes the settings read by the view, and translate becomes a host route that names an event and a block instead of carrying text.

ctx.pluginRecommendations has one remote method, describe, which returns catalogue text for a card. With no card there is nothing to describe; the feature-guide skill reads the catalogue from area A21's plugins.Manager directly.

ctx.translator becomes the service key translate.Key with the interface Service: Providers, Lookup and Translate. resolve and translate merge into one call that takes a fragment reference instead of text, and availableProviders becomes Providers with a reason for each unavailable one.

Kept: translation is for display only and never replaces stored output or enters model input; the provider is explicit and a failure never picks another receiver; only an expanded body starts translation. Changed: enabling the bundle is no longer consent and Bing is no longer preselected. The web endpoints are a registered sender that needs a permit, its own setting and an explicit provider choice, because the text is model output sent to a third party (DH-ADR-9).

The rules are kept: one fresh text-only request per fragment with no history and no tools, the exact request written to the session before it is sent, and no fallback. The mechanism changes: instead of two built-in vendor routes and one exact model id, the model provider uses a configured route whose default is the session's own logged route, so by default the text returns to the provider that produced it; and the call gets exactly one outcome event with usage.

Kept: requests and results live in the session they belong to, the request is durable before dispatch and the result before display, and a result is reused only for the same text, languages, provider and recipe. Changed: they are declared ignorable event types instead of plugin records, the host reads the source text from the committed event instead of trusting the browser, a fold replaces the log scan, and nothing activates a session to write a record.

The note keeps npm package names and config row ids stable when packages move into the experimental directory, so that installed Web and Desktop profiles keep working. Go has no npm names and is not required to load upstream profiles (DH-ADR-2). The lesson is kept as a rule: ids in config and names in the log carry no maturity marker, so promoting a feature renames nothing a user or a session refers to.

The note proposes, and upstream has not built, a bridge that imports another harness's TypeScript extension sources into the host process, where they run with the host's full authority and hook its events in process. DH-ADR-4 rules out loading code into the host, and a plugin process cannot intercept host events, so the Go design builds no such bridge and nothing in it depends on one.

The note itself recommends building nothing now, because the other project's plugin interface is unpublished and unstable, and describes six levels to revisit later. Go also builds nothing: every level above zero runs a JavaScript composition runtime in or beside the host, which DH-ADR-4 would make a separate process, and no Go deliverable depends on it.
